overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Merleau-Ponty's critique of classical theories of perception. You'll be asked about pure sensation, association, attention, judgment, and the error shared by empiricism and intellectualism.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: Why does Merleau-Ponty say that a pure sensation is never perceived?

options.html: Because sensations are too faint for us to notice them
options.text: Because sensations are too faint for us to notice them
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The point isn't faintness. Even the simplest perception is already a figure on a ground, so an isolated sensation is never given.

options.html: Because even the simplest datum is a figure on a ground
options.text: Because even the simplest datum is a figure on a ground
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A white patch on a uniform background already has a contour that belongs to it. A sensation without a field is a theoretical construction.

options.html: Because the brain processes sensations before we're aware
options.text: Because the brain processes sensations before we're aware
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Merleau-Ponty's argument is descriptive, not neurological. Even the simplest datum is a figure on a ground.

options.html: Because sensations exist only in the objective world
options.text: Because sensations exist only in the objective world
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The argument is that even the simplest perceived datum is a figure on a ground, so pure sensation is never given.

forms.stemHtml: Walking along a beach, you see masts and a funnel merge with the trees behind them until, suddenly, a beached ship appears. Why does this trouble the empiricist account?

options.html: Because the ship is too far away to produce sensations
options.text: Because the ship is too far away to produce sensations
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Nothing new reaches the eyes. The whole field reorganizes, which association and memory can't explain.

options.html: Because the observer has judged the scene incorrectly
options.text: Because the observer has judged the scene incorrectly
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's closer to the intellectualist story. The problem for empiricism is that the field reorganizes without new sensations.

options.html: Because the field reorganizes without any new sensations
options.text: Because the field reorganizes without any new sensations
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The change isn't in the stimuli or in a recalled memory. It's in the organization of the whole field.

options.html: Because memory supplies the image of the ship directly
options.text: Because memory supplies the image of the ship directly
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Merleau-Ponty argues that memory can't supply the meaning of the present. The field reorganizes on its own.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are claims Merleau-Ponty makes about empiricism and intellectualism? (Select all that apply.)

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! In both, attention only uncovers a content that was already complete.

options.html: Both read the objective world into perception
options.text: Both read the objective world into perception
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This is the prejudice of the world, which both theories share.

options.html: The judgment view can't explain persistent illusions
options.text: The judgment view can't explain persistent illusions
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The Müller-Lyer lines still look unequal after we know they're equal.

options.html: The truth lies somewhere between the two theories
options.text: The truth lies somewhere between the two theories
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Merleau-Ponty rejects the premise both theories share. He doesn't split the difference.

options.html: Empirical science should be ignored in philosophy
options.text: Empirical science should be ignored in philosophy
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Merleau-Ponty uses experimental findings extensively. He rejects explanations that replace the phenomenon with a theory.

forms.stemHtml: What is Merleau-Ponty's term for the view that perception is the work of a mind that attends, judges, and constitutes objects, so that perceiving is a form of thinking? Enter one word.

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Intellectualism has too much mind in perception, just as empiricism has too little.
Sorry, that's incorrect. Empiricism builds perception from sensations. The view that perceiving is a form of thinking is intellectualism.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The view that perceiving is a form of thinking is intellectualism.

forms.stemHtml: What does Merleau-Ponty mean by the "prejudice of the world"?

options.html: The tendency to trust other people's descriptions of the world
options.text: The tendency to trust other people's descriptions of the world
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The prejudice of the world is the assumption that the determinate world of science is given first and read back into perception.

options.html: The belief that the external world might not exist at all
options.text: The belief that the external world might not exist at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's skepticism. The prejudice of the world is the assumption that the determinate world of science comes first.

options.html: Assuming the measured world comes first and reading it into perception
options.text: Assuming the measured world comes first and reading it into perception
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Empiricism puts that world into sensations, and intellectualism puts it into thought. Both start from it.

options.html: The social biases that shape how we see different groups
options.text: The social biases that shape how we see different groups
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The prejudice of the world concerns the theory of perception: assuming the determinate world of science comes first.

title: Beyond Empiricism and Intellectualism
